<title>Epidemiology of breast cancer</title>
<fragment>
![](image)Age-standardized deaths from breast cancer per 100,000 inhabitants in 2004.[1] |  |  |  |

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]




## By age group

[edit]

Breast cancer is strongly related to age, with only 5% of all breast cancers occurring in women under 40 years old.[6]

The lifetime risk for breast cancer in the United States is usually given as about 1 in 8 (12%) of women by age 95, with a 1 in 35 (3%) chance of dying from breast cancer.[10] This calculation assumes that all women live to at least age 95, except for those who die from breast cancer before age 95.[11] Recent work, using real-world numbers, indicate that the actual risk is probably less than half the theoretical risk.[12]

<title>Cervical cancer</title>
<fragment>
Worldwide, cervical cancer is both the fourth-most common type of cancer and the fourth-most common cause of death from cancer in women.[3] In 2012, an estimated 528,000 cases of cervical cancer occurred, with 266,000 deaths.[3] This is about 8% of the total cases and total deaths from cancer.[21] About 70% of cervical cancers and 90% of deaths occur in developing countries.[3][22] In low-income countries, it is one of the most common causes of cancer death with an incidence rate of 47.3 per 100,000 women.[23][19] In developed countries, the widespread use of cervical screening programs has dramatically reduced rates of cervical cancer.[24] Expected scenarios for the reduction of mortality due to cervical cancer worldwide (and specially in low-income countries) have been reviewed, given assumptions with respect to the achievement of recommended prevention targets using triple-intervention strategies defined by WHO.[25] In medical research, the most famous immortalized cell line, known as HeLa,

Worldwide, cervical cancer is both the fourth-most common cause of cancer and deaths from cancer in women.[3] In 2018, 570,000 cases of cervical cancer were estimated to have occurred, with over 300,000 deaths.[121] It is the second-most common cause of female-specific cancer after breast cancer, accounting for around 8% of both total cancer cases and total cancer deaths in women.[21] About 80% of cervical cancers occur in developing countries.[122] It is the most frequently detected cancer during pregnancy, with an occurrence of 1.5 to 12 for every 100,000 pregnancies.[123]

The risks from developing specific types of ovarian cancer varies. Germ cell tumors and sex cord-stromal tumors are less common than epithelial tumors. The number of new cases a year in the US is 0.4 per 100,000 women and 0.2 per 100,000 women, respectively. In young people, sex-cord stromal tumors and germ cell tumors total 1% of overall ovarian cancer.[33] Ovarian cancer represents approximately 4% of cancers diagnosed in women.[31]



### United Kingdom

[edit]

It is the 5th-most common cancer in UK women (around 7,100 were diagnosed in 2011) and the 5th-most common cause of cancer death in women (around 4,300 died in 2012).[134][31][35] The incidence rate over the whole UK population is 21.6 per 100,000.


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Ovarian cancer cases diagnosed by age group in the US[124]
![](image)Ovarian cancer by age and type.[130]
In 2022, in the United States, an estimated 19,880 new cases were diagnosed and 12,810 women died of ovarian cancer.[131] The 5-year relative survival rate is 49.7%.[132] Around 57% cases have metastasized at the time of diagnosis.[132]


In 2014, over 220,000 diagnoses of epithelial ovarian cancer were made yearly.[28] The overall lifetime risk in the US is around 1.6%[26][31] In the US, ovarian cancer affects 1.3–1.4% and is the cause of death of about 1% of women.[29][133] In the United States, it is also the fifth-most common cancer in women but the fourth-most common cause of cancer death.[31] This decrease made it the ninth-most common cancer in women.[29]


</fragment>

<document>
<title>Women's health</title>
<fragment>
Women and men have approximately equal risk of dying from cancer, which accounts for about a quarter of all deaths, and is the second leading cause of death. However the relative incidence of different cancers varies between women and men. Globally the three most common types of cancer of women in 2020 were breast, lung and colorectal cancers. These three account for 44.5% of all cancer cases in women. Other types of cancers specifically affecting women include ovarian, uterine (endometrial and cervical) cancers.[126]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Breast cancer is most common type of cancer among women. Globally, it accounts for 25% of all cancers.[126] It is also among the ten most common chronic diseases of women, and a substantial contributor to loss of quality of life.[8] In 2016, breast cancer was the most common cancer diagnosed among women in both developed and developing countries, accounting for nearly 30% of all cases, and worldwide accounts for one and a half million cases and over half a million deaths, being the fifth most common cause of cancer death overall and the second in developed regions. Geographic variation in incidence is the opposite of that of cervical cancer, being highest in Northern America and lowest in Eastern and Middle Africa, but mortality rates are relatively constant, resulting in a wide variance in case mortality, ranging from 25% in developed regions to 37% in developing regions, and with 62% of deaths occurring in developing countries.[19][128]



#### Cervical cancer

[edit]

Main article: Cervical cancer


</fragment>
<fragment>
* Siegel, Rebecca L.; Miller, Kimberly D.; Jemal, Ahmedin (January 2016). "Cancer statistics, 2016". *CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians*. **66** (1): 7–30. doi:10.3322/caac.21332. PMID 26742998.}
* Stevens, Gretchen A; Mathers, Colin D; Beard, John R (1 September 2013). "Global mortality trends and patterns in older women". *Bulletin of the World Health Organization*. **91** (9): 630–639. doi:10.2471/BLT.12.109710. PMC 3790210. PMID 24101779.
* Turshen, Meredeth; Koblinsky, Marge; Timyan, Judith; Gay, Jill (December 1994). "The Health of Women: A Global Perspective". *Journal of Public Health Policy*. **14** (3): 366. doi:10.2307/3343047. JSTOR 3343047. S2CID 71078396.

</fragment>
<fragment>

While the rates of the leading causes of death, cardiovascular disease, cancer and lung disease, are similar in women and men, women have different experiences. Lung cancer has overtaken all other types of cancer as the leading cause of cancer related death in women, followed by breast cancer, colorectal, ovarian, uterine and cervical cancers. While smoking is the major cause of lung cancer, amongst nonsmoking women the risk of developing cancer is three times greater than among nonsmoking men. Despite this, breast cancer remains the most common cancer in women in developed countries, and is one of the major chronic diseases of women, while cervical cancer remains one of the most common cancers in developing countries, associated with human papilloma virus (HPV), a sexually transmitted disease. HPV vaccine together with screening offers the promise of controlling these diseases. Other important health issues for women include cardiovascular disease, depression, dementia, osteoporosis and anemia. 


</fragment>
</document>

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles, here's what I found about the leading causes of death among women globally:

## Leading Causes of Death in Women

### Cardiovascular Disease (Heart Disease)
- **Leading cause**: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death globally among women (and men)
- Overall, cardiovascular disease causes more than 17 million deaths worldwide (about 31% of total deaths)
- Women and men have similar mortality rates from cardiovascular disease, though women may experience symptoms differently

### Cancer
- Cancer accounts for about a quarter of all deaths and is the second leading cause of death
- Women and men have approximately equal risk of dying from cancer overall
- However, different cancer types predominate in women:

**Most Common Cancers in Women (2020):**
1. **Breast cancer** - Accounts for 25% of all cancers in women globally
2. **Lung cancer** - Has become the leading cause of cancer-related death in women
3. **Colorectal cancer** - The second most common cause of cancer in women (9.2% of diagnoses)

**Other significant cancers affecting women:**
- Ovarian cancer
- Uterine (endometrial and cervical) cancers
- Cervical cancer remains particularly common in developing countries

### Other Leading Causes
- **Lung diseases** - Among the top three leading causes with similar rates in women and men
- **Dementia/Alzheimer's disease** - More common in women than men, largely due to women's longer life expectancy
- **Stomach cancer** - Eighth most common cancer globally

### Key Regional Differences:
- **Developed countries**: Breast cancer is most common, cervical cancer less prevalent
- **Developing countries**: Cervical cancer remains one of the most common cancers, associated with HPV infection

### Notable Points:
- The three leading causes of death (cardiovascular disease, cancer, and lung disease) have similar rates in women and men
- Geographic variations exist in incidence and mortality rates for specific diseases
- Many leading causes are preventable through lifestyle changes, screening, and vaccination (like HPV vaccine for cervical cancer)

The information reflects global patterns, though specific rankings may vary by country, region, and socioeconomic factors.

<document>
<title>Cancer</title>
<fragment>
Estimates are that in 2018, 18.1 million new cases of cancer and 9.6 million deaths occur globally.[211] About 20% of males and 17% of females will get cancer at some point in time while 13% of males and 9% of females will die from it.[211]


In 2008, approximately 12.7 million cancers were diagnosed (excluding non-melanoma skin cancers and other non-invasive cancers)[25] and in 2010 nearly 7.98 million people died.[212] Cancers account for approximately 16% of deaths. The most common as of 2018[update] are lung cancer (1.76 million deaths), colorectal cancer (860,000) stomach cancer (780,000), liver cancer (780,000), and breast cancer (620,000).[2] This makes invasive cancer the leading cause of death in the developed world and the second leading in the developing world.[25] Over half of cases occur in the developing world.[25]


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)Three measures of global cancer mortality from 1990 to 2017[203]
Survival rates vary by cancer type and by the stage at which it is diagnosed, ranging from majority survival to complete mortality five years after diagnosis. Once a cancer has metastasized, prognosis normally becomes much worse. About half of patients receiving treatment for invasive cancer (excluding carcinoma *in situ* and non-melanoma skin cancers) die from that cancer or its treatment.[25] A majority of cancer deaths are due to metastases of the primary tumor.[204]


Survival is worse in the developing world,[25] partly because the types of cancer that are most common there are harder to treat than those associated with developed countries.[205]


</fragment>
<fragment>
the average five-year survival rate is 66% for all ages.[5]


In 2015, about 90.5 million people worldwide had cancer.[18] In 2019, annual cancer cases grew by 23.6 million people and there were 10 million deaths worldwide, representing over the previous decade increases of 26% and 21%, respectively.[6][19]


</fragment>

The most common types of cancer in males are lung cancer, prostate cancer, colorectal cancer, and stomach cancer.[20][21] In females, the most common types are breast cancer, colorectal cancer, lung cancer, and cervical cancer.[10][22] If skin cancer other than melanoma were included in total new cancer cases each year, it would account for around 40% of cases.[23][24] In children, acute lymphoblastic leukemia and brain tumors are most common, except in Africa, where non-Hodgkin lymphoma occurs more often.[17] In 2012, about 165,000 children under 15 years of age were diagnosed with cancer.[20] The risk of cancer increases significantly with age, and many cancers occur more commonly in developed countries.[10] Rates are increasing as more people live to an old age and as lifestyle changes occur in the developing world.[25] The global total economic costs of cancer were estimated at US$1.16 trillion (equivalent to $1.67 trillion in 2024) per year as of 2010[update].[26]

<document>
<title>Epidemiology of cancer</title>
<fragment>
In Canada, as of 2007, cancer is the number one cause of death, contributing to 29.6% of all deaths in the country. The second highest cause of death is cardiovascular diseases resulting in 21.5% of deaths. As of 2011, prostate cancer was the most common form of cancer among males (about 28% of all new cases) and breast cancer the most common in females (also about 28% of all new cases).[*citation needed*]


The leading cause of death in both males and females is lung cancer, which contributes to 26.8% of all cancer deaths. Statistics indicate that between the ages of 20 and 50 years, the incidence rate of cancer is higher amongst women whereas after 50 years of age, the incidence rate increases in men. Predictions by the Canadian Cancer Society indicate that with time, there will be an increase in the rates of incidence of cancer for both males and females. Cancer will thus continue to be a persistent issue in years to come.[*citation needed*]



### United States

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
According to the National Cancer Registry Programme of the India Council of Medical Research (ICMR), more than 1300 Indians die every day due to cancer. Between 2012 and 2014, the mortality rate due to cancer increased by approximately 6%. In 2012, there were 478,180 deaths out of 2,934,314 cases reported. In 2013 there were 465,169 deaths out of 3,016,628 cases. In 2014, 491,598 people died in out of 2,820,179 cases.[23]
According to the Population Cancer Registry of Indian Council of Medical Research, the incidence and mortality of cancer is highest in the north-eastern region of the country.[24] Breast cancer is the most common, and stomach cancer is the leading cause of death by cancer for the population as a whole. Breast cancer and lung cancer kill the most women and men respectively.[25]



### Canada

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Cancer is responsible for about 25% of all deaths in the U.S., and is a major public health problem in many parts of the world. The statistics below are estimates for the U.S. in 2008, and may vary substantially in other countries. They exclude basal and squamous cell skin cancers, and carcinoma in situ in locations other than the urinary bladder.[20] As seen, breast/prostate cancer, lung cancer and colorectal cancer are responsible for approximately half of cancer incidence. The same applies for cancer mortality, but with lung cancer replacing breast/prostate cancer as the main cause.[*citation needed*]


In 2016, an estimated 1,685,210 new cases of cancer will be diagnosed in the United States and 595,690 people will die from the disease.[28]



* ![Most common cancers in US males, by occurrence[20]](image)

Most common cancers in US males, by occurrence[20]
* ![in US males, by mortality[20]](image)

in US males, by mortality[20]


* ![in US females, by occurrence[20]](image)


</fragment>
<fragment>
![](image)New cancer diagnosis in the England in 2012
In the U.S. cancer is second only to cardiovascular disease as the leading cause of death;[20] in the UK it is the leading cause of death.[21] In many developing countries cancer incidence (insofar as this can be measured) appears much lower, most likely because of the higher death rates due to infectious disease or injury. With the increased control over malaria and tuberculosis in some Third World countries, incidence of cancer is expected to rise; in the Eastern Mediterranean region, for example, cancer incidence is expected to increase by 100% to 180% in the next 15 years due to increases in life expectancy, an increasing proportion of elderly people, and the successful control of childhood disease.[22] This is termed the epidemiologic transition in epidemiological terminology.[*citation needed*]


</fragment>
</document>

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]




## By age group

[edit]

Breast cancer is strongly related to age, with only 5% of all breast cancers occurring in women under 40 years old.[6]

<title>Cervical cancer</title>
<fragment>
As of 2022, the World Health Organization announced that "each year in the WHO European Region more than 66 000 women are newly diagnosed with cervical cancer and more than 30 000 die from this preventable disease."[132]



### United Kingdom

[edit]



|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| ![](image)
 | This section needs to be **updated**. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information. *(September 2021)*
 |


Cervical cancer is the 12th-most common cancer in women in the UK (around 3,100 women were diagnosed with the disease in 2011), and accounts for 1% of cancer deaths (around 920 died in 2012).[133] With a 42% reduction from 1988 to 1997, the NHS-implemented screening programme has been highly successful, screening the highest-risk age group (25–49 years) every 3 years, and those ages 50–64 every 5 years.[*citation needed*]



### United States

[edit]




</fragment>
<fragment>
Worldwide, cervical cancer is both the fourth-most common type of cancer and the fourth-most common cause of death from cancer in women.[3] In 2012, an estimated 528,000 cases of cervical cancer occurred, with 266,000 deaths.[3] This is about 8% of the total cases and total deaths from cancer.[21] About 70% of cervical cancers and 90% of deaths occur in developing countries.[3][22] In low-income countries, it is one of the most common causes of cancer death with an incidence rate of 47.3 per 100,000 women.[23][19] In developed countries, the widespread use of cervical screening programs has dramatically reduced rates of cervical cancer.[24] Expected scenarios for the reduction of mortality due to cervical cancer worldwide (and specially in low-income countries) have been reviewed, given assumptions with respect to the achievement of recommended prevention targets using triple-intervention strategies defined by WHO.[25] In medical research, the most famous immortalized cell line, known as HeLa,

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]

Survival rates vary by cancer type and by the stage at which it is diagnosed, ranging from majority survival to complete mortality five years after diagnosis. In 2022, in the United States, an estimated 19,880 new cases were diagnosed and 12,810 women died of ovarian cancer.[131] The 5-year relative survival rate is 49.7%.[132] Around 57% cases have metastasized at the time of diagnosis.[132]


In 2014, over 220,000 diagnoses of epithelial ovarian cancer were made yearly.[28] The overall lifetime risk in the US is around 1.6%[26][31] In the US, ovarian cancer affects 1.3–1.4% and is the cause of death of about 1% of women.[29][133] In the United States, it is also the fifth-most common cancer in women but the fourth-most common cause of cancer death.[31] This decrease made it the ninth-most common cancer in women.[29]

### PanNETs

[edit]

<fragment>
Pancreatic cancer is among the most deadly forms of cancer globally, with one of the lowest survival rates. In 2015, pancreatic cancers of all types resulted in 411,600 deaths globally.[8] Pancreatic cancer is the fifth-most-common cause of death from cancer in the United Kingdom,[17] and the third most-common in the United States.[18] The disease occurs most often in the developed world, where about 70% of the new cases in 2012 originated.[10] Pancreatic adenocarcinoma typically has a very poor prognosis; after diagnosis, 25% of people survive one year and 12% live for five years.[6][10] For cancers diagnosed early, the five-year survival rate rises to about 20%.[19] Neuroendocrine cancers have better outcomes; at five years from diagnosis, 65% of those diagnosed are living, though survival considerably varies depending on the type of tumor.[10]

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles for cancer statistics, here are the top 10 countries with the highest cancer rates worldwide and the most common cancer types:

## Top 10 Countries with Highest Cancer Rates (per 100,000 population)

According to 2018 GLOBOCAN statistics (age-standardized rates):

1. **Australia**: 468.0
2. **New Zealand**: 438.1  
3. **Ireland**: 373.7
4. **Hungary**: 368.1
5. **United States**: 352.2
6. **Belgium**: 345.8
7. **France**: 344.1
8. **Denmark**: 340.4
9. **Norway**: 337.8
10. **Netherlands**: 334.1

## Most Common Cancer Types Globally

### By Incidence (New Cases):

1. **Lung Cancer** - Most diagnosed cancer worldwide
   - 2.2 million new cases in 2020
   - Leading cause of cancer death

2. **Breast Cancer** - Most common invasive cancer in women
   - 2.09 million cases (2018)
   - Affects 1 in 7 women globally
   - Along with lung cancer, most commonly diagnosed overall

3. **Prostate Cancer** - Major cancer in men
   - Varies significantly by country/region
   - More common in developed nations

### By Mortality (Deaths):

1. **Lung Cancer** - Deadliest cancer
   - 1.8 million deaths in 2020 (18% of all cancer deaths)
   - Expected to rise to nearly 3 million annual deaths by 2035

2. **Breast Cancer** - Second leading cause in women
   - 458,503 deaths worldwide (2008)

3. **Pancreatic Cancer** - Among most deadly
   - 411,600 deaths globally (2015)
   - 5th most common cause of cancer death in UK, 3rd in US
   - Extremely poor prognosis: only 12% survive 5 years

## Key Patterns:

- **Geographic Variation**: Australia and other developed nations have the highest overall cancer rates
- **Developed vs. Developing**: Cancer incidence is generally higher in developed countries
- **Survival Rates**: Vary dramatically by cancer type - lung and pancreatic cancers have very poor survival rates, while prostate and breast cancers (when detected early) have much better outcomes
- **Smoking Impact**: Lung cancer's dominance in mortality is largely due to tobacco use

Note: Non-melanoma skin cancer, while very common, is often excluded from these statistics as it's typically non-invasive and easily treated.

As of 2022, the World Health Organization announced that "each year in the WHO European Region more than 66 000 women are newly diagnosed with cervical cancer and more than 30 000 die from this preventable disease."[132]



### United Kingdom

[edit]

Cervical cancer is the 12th-most common cancer in women in the UK (around 3,100 women were diagnosed with the disease in 2011), and accounts for 1% of cancer deaths (around 920 died in 2012).[133] With a 42% reduction from 1988 to 1997, the NHS-implemented screening programme has been highly successful, screening the highest-risk age group (25–49 years) every 3 years, and those ages 50–64 every 5 years.[*citation needed*]

Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases in 2020 resulting in 1.8 million deaths.[3] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; the average age at diagnosis is 70 years, and the average age at death 72.[2] Incidence and outcomes vary widely across the world, depending on patterns of tobacco use. Prior to the advent of cigarette smoking in the 20th century, lung cancer was a rare disease. In the 1950s and 1960s, increasing evidence linked lung cancer and tobacco use, culminating in declarations by most large national health bodies discouraging tobacco use.

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most-common invasive cancer in women.[199] Along with lung cancer, breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer, with 2.09 million cases each in 2018.[200] Breast cancer affects 1 in 7 (14%) of women worldwide.[201] (The most common form of cancer is non-invasive non-melanoma skin cancer; non-invasive cancers are generally easily cured, cause very few deaths, and are routinely excluded from cancer statistics.) Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[202] and 16% of all female cancers.[203] In 2012, it comprised 25.2% of cancers diagnosed in women, making it the most-common female cancer.[204]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide (13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together).[202] Lung cancer, the second most-common cause of cancer-related deaths in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women (18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together).[202]


The incidence of breast cancer varies greatly around the world: it is lowest in less-developed countries and greatest in the more-developed countries. In the twelve world regions, the annual age-standardized incidence rates per 100,000 women are as follows: 18 in Eastern Asia, 22 in South Central Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, 26 in South-Eastern Asia, 26, 28 in North Africa and Western Asia, 42 in South and Central America, 42, 49 in Eastern Europe, 56 in Southern Europe, 73 in Northern Europe, 74 in Oceania, 78 in Western Europe, and 90 in North America.[205] Metastatic breast cancer affects between 19% (United States) and 50% (parts of Africa) of women with breast cancer.[206]

<title>Epidemiology of cancer</title>
<fragment>
In Canada, as of 2007, cancer is the number one cause of death, contributing to 29.6% of all deaths in the country. The second highest cause of death is cardiovascular diseases resulting in 21.5% of deaths. As of 2011, prostate cancer was the most common form of cancer among males (about 28% of all new cases) and breast cancer the most common in females (also about 28% of all new cases).[*citation needed*]


The leading cause of death in both males and females is lung cancer, which contributes to 26.8% of all cancer deaths. Statistics indicate that between the ages of 20 and 50 years, the incidence rate of cancer is higher amongst women whereas after 50 years of age, the incidence rate increases in men. Predictions by the Canadian Cancer Society indicate that with time, there will be an increase in the rates of incidence of cancer for both males and females. Cancer will thus continue to be a persistent issue in years to come.[*citation needed*]



### United States

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
According to the National Cancer Registry Programme of the India Council of Medical Research (ICMR), more than 1300 Indians die every day due to cancer. Between 2012 and 2014, the mortality rate due to cancer increased by approximately 6%. In 2012, there were 478,180 deaths out of 2,934,314 cases reported. In 2013 there were 465,169 deaths out of 3,016,628 cases. In 2014, 491,598 people died in out of 2,820,179 cases.[23]
According to the Population Cancer Registry of Indian Council of Medical Research, the incidence and mortality of cancer is highest in the north-eastern region of the country.[24] Breast cancer is the most common, and stomach cancer is the leading cause of death by cancer for the population as a whole. Breast cancer and lung cancer kill the most women and men respectively.[25]



### Canada

[edit]

<title>Breast cancer</title>
<fragment>

In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide (13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together).[202] Lung cancer, the second most-common cause of cancer-related deaths in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women (18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together).[202]


The incidence of breast cancer varies greatly around the world: it is lowest in less-developed countries and greatest in the more-developed countries. In the twelve world regions, the annual age-standardized incidence rates per 100,000 women are as follows: 18 in Eastern Asia, 22 in South Central Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, 26 in South-Eastern Asia, 26, 28 in North Africa and Western Asia, 42 in South and Central America, 42, 49 in Eastern Europe, 56 in Southern Europe, 73 in Northern Europe, 74 in Oceania, 78 in Western Europe, and 90 in North America.[205] Metastatic breast cancer affects between 19% (United States) and 50% (parts of Africa) of women with breast cancer.[206]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In 2002 it was noted that as a result of breast cancer's high visibility, the statistical results can be misinterpreted, such as the claim that one in eight women will be diagnosed with breast cancer during their lives – a claim that depends on the unrealistic assumption that no woman will die of any other disease before the age of 95.[220]: 199–200 By 2010 the breast cancer survival rate in Europe was 91% at one years and 65% at five years. In the USA the five-year survival rate for localized breast cancer was 96.8%, while in cases of metastases it was only 20.6%. Because the prognosis for breast cancer was at this stage relatively favorable, compared to the prognosis for other cancers, breast cancer as cause of death among women was 13.9% of all cancer deaths. The second most common cause of death from cancer in women was lung cancer, the most common cancer worldwide for men and women. The improved survival rate made breast cancer the most prevalent cancer in the world.

<title>Lung cancer</title>
<fragment>
Worldwide, lung cancer is the most diagnosed type of cancer, and the leading cause of cancer death.[94][95] In 2020, 2.2 million new cases were diagnosed, and 1.8 million people died from lung cancer, representing 18% of all cancer deaths.[3] Lung cancer deaths are expected to rise globally to nearly 3 million annual deaths by 2035, due to high rates of tobacco use and aging populations.[95] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; after that, cancer rates increase with age, stabilizing around age 80.[1] The median age of a person diagnosed with lung cancer is 70; the median age of death is 72.[2]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases in 2020 resulting in 1.8 million deaths.[3] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; the average age at diagnosis is 70 years, and the average age at death 72.[2] Incidence and outcomes vary widely across the world, depending on patterns of tobacco use. Prior to the advent of cigarette smoking in the 20th century, lung cancer was a rare disease. In the 1950s and 1960s, increasing evidence linked lung cancer and tobacco use, culminating in declarations by most large national health bodies discouraging tobacco use.




## Signs and symptoms

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Lung cancer incidence varies by geography and sex, with the highest rates in Micronesia, Polynesia, Europe, Asia, and North America; and lowest rates in Africa and Central America.[96] Globally, around 8% of men and 6% of women develop lung cancer in their lifetimes.[1] The ratio of lung cancer cases in men to women varies considerably by geography, from as high as nearly 12:1 in Belarus, to 1:1 in Brazil, likely due to differences in smoking patterns.[97]

Based on the information I found from Wikipedia articles, here are the leading causes of cancer death among women globally:

## **Main Cancer Death Causes in Women (Global Statistics)**

### **1. Lung Cancer**
- **Leading cause**: Lung cancer is the overall leading cause of cancer death in women globally
- **Statistics**: In 2008, lung cancer caused 13.7% of cancer deaths in women (18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women combined)
- **2020 Global Data**: 2.2 million new cases diagnosed worldwide, with 1.8 million deaths (18% of all cancer deaths)
- **Note**: Breast cancer is often more commonly diagnosed, but lung cancer is more fatal

### **2. Breast Cancer**
- **High incidence but better survival**: While breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women, it has better survival rates than lung cancer
- **2008 Deaths**: Caused 13.7% of cancer deaths in women (same as lung cancer for that year)
- **2020 Prevalence**: Second most commonly diagnosed cancer alongside lung cancer, with both having about 2.09 million cases each
- **Survival advantage**: Better prognosis compared to lung cancer, making it the most prevalent cancer in terms of people living with it

### **3. Cervical Cancer**
- **Fourth most common cause**: Worldwide, cervical cancer is the fourth-most common cause of cancer death in women
- **2012 Statistics**: 528,000 cases with 266,000 deaths (about 8% of total cancer deaths in women)
- **2018 Data**: 570,000 cases with over 300,000 deaths
- **Geographic disparity**: About 70-80% of deaths occur in developing countries

## **Regional Variations**
- **Canada (as of 2007)**: Lung cancer was the leading cause of cancer death for both men and women (26.8% of all cancer deaths)
- **India**: Breast cancer kills the most women, followed by lung cancer
- **Developed vs Developing**: Developed countries have better screening and treatment, leading to lower mortality rates, particularly for breast and cervical cancers

## **Important Notes**
- Tobacco use is the primary driver behind lung cancer's high mortality rate
- Improved screening programs have reduced cervical cancer deaths significantly in developed countries
- Breast cancer's high survival rate makes it the most prevalent cancer (most people living with it) even while lung cancer remains more deadly

The data shows that **lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in women globally**, despite breast cancer being more commonly diagnosed. Cervical cancer ranks fourth in cancer mortality among women worldwide.

基于我对全球癌症死亡统计数据的查阅，**肺癌是全球女性癌症死亡的首要原因**。以下是按死亡率从高到低的详细信息：

## **♥️ 全球女性癌症死亡主要原因**

### **1. 肺癌 (首位)**
- **死亡统计**：2008年导致女性13.7%的癌症死亡
- **2020年数据**：全球220万新发病例中，180万例死亡（占所有癌症死亡的18%）
- **特点**：虽然乳腺癌诊断率更高，但肺癌的致死性最强
- **主要原因**：吸烟是主要驱动因素

### **2. 乳腺癌 (第二位)**
- **死亡统计**：2008年同样导致女性13.7%的癌症死亡
- **全球发病率**：是最常见的女性癌症，全球每7名女性中就有1人患病（14%）
- **生存优势**：相比肺癌预后更好，5年生存率相对较高
- **2020年**：约209万新发病例（与肺癌并列）

### **3. 结直肠癌 (第三位)**  
- **死亡统计**：是女性第四大常见癌症死亡原因
- **2012年数据**：占女性癌症诊断的9.2%
- **死亡率差异**：发达国家较低，发展中国家较高

### **4. 宫颈癌 (第四位)**
- **死亡统计**：全球女性癌症死亡的第四大原因
- **2018年数据**：57万新发病例，30万+死亡
- **地区差异**：70-80%的死亡发生在发展中国家
- **可预防性**：通过筛查和疫苗可显著降低死亡率

## **🌍 地区差异**

### **发达国家**：
- 肺癌仍居首位
- 乳腺癌、宫颈癌死亡率显著降低（得益于筛查和治疗进步）

### **发展中国家**：
- 乳腺癌死亡率上升最快
- 宫颈癌死亡率远高于发达国家
- 总体癌症死亡率呈上升趋势

## **📊 关键统计数据**

- **全球总体**：乳腺癌是女性最常见的癌症，但肺癌是最致命的
- **2008年对比**：肺癌和乳腺癌各占女性癌症死亡的13.7%
- **生存现状**：乳腺癌 因较高的生存率成为现患病例最多的癌症

这组数据揭示了癌症控制中的一个重要现象：**高发病率不等于高死亡率**。肺癌虽然在女性中的发病率低于乳腺癌，但由于其侵袭性强、早期诊断困难，仍然是导致女性癌症死亡的首要原因。

- **2020年数据**：全球220万新发病例中，180万例死亡（占所有癌症死亡的18%）
- **特点**：虽然乳腺癌诊断率更高，但肺癌的致死性最强
- **主要原因**：吸烟是主要驱动因素

### **2. 乳腺癌 (第二位)**
- **死亡统计**：2008年同样导致女性13.7%的癌症死亡
- **全球发病率**：是最常见的女性癌症，全球每7名女性中就有1人患病（14%）
- **生存优势**：相比肺癌预后更好，5年生存率相对较高
- **2020年**：约209万新发病例（与肺癌并列）

### **3. 结直肠癌 (第三位)**  
- **死亡统计**：是女性第四大常见癌症死亡原因
- **2012年数据**：占女性癌症诊断的9.2%
- **死亡率差异**：发达国家较低，发展中国家较高

### **4. 宫颈癌 (第四位)**
- **死亡统计**：全球女性癌症死亡的第四大原因
- **2018年数据**：57万新发病例，30万+死亡
- **地区差异**：70-80%的死亡发生在发展中国家
- **可预防性**：通过筛查和疫苗可显著降低死亡率

## **🌍 地区差异**

### **发达国家**：
- 肺癌仍居首位
- 乳腺癌、宫颈癌死亡率显著降低（得益于筛查和治疗进步）

### **发展中国家**：
- 乳腺癌死亡率上升最快
- 宫颈癌死亡率远高于发达国家
- 总体癌症死亡率呈上升趋势

## **📊 关键统计数据**

- **全球总体**：乳腺癌是女性最常见的癌症，但肺癌是最致命的
- **2008年对比**：肺癌和乳腺癌各占女性癌症死亡的13.7%
- **生存现状**：乳腺癌 因较高的生存率成为现患病例最多的癌症

这组数据揭示了癌症控制中的一个重要现象：**高发病率不等于高死亡率**。肺癌虽然在女性中的发病率低于乳腺癌，但由于其侵袭性强、早期诊断困难，仍然是导致女性癌症死亡的首要原因。

Globally pancreatic cancer is the 11th most common cancer in women and the 12th most common in men.[10] The majority of recorded cases occur in developed countries.[10] People from the United States have an average lifetime risk of about 1 in 67 (or 1.5%) of developing the disease,[112] slightly higher than the figure for the UK.[113] The disease is more common in men than women,[2][10] though the difference in rates has narrowed over recent decades, probably reflecting earlier increases in female smoking. In the United States the risk for African Americans is over 50% greater than for whites, but the rates in Africa and East Asia are much lower than those in North America or Europe. Based on information gathered from Wikipedia articles on major cancers, here are the most common cancers affecting women worldwide:

## Leading Cancers in Women

### 1. **Breast Cancer**
- **Most common cancer globally in women**
- Leading cause of cancer death in women in many regions
- Affects women of all ages, though risk increases with age
- High survival rates when detected early

### 2. **Lung Cancer**
- Second most common cancer in women globally
- Leading cause of cancer death in women in developed countries
- Historically more common in men, but rates in women have been rising, largely due to smoking patterns

### 3. **Colorectal Cancer**
- Third most common cancer in women
- Affects the colon and rectum
- Strong correlation with diet, lifestyle, and age

### 4. **Pancreatic Cancer**
- 11th most common cancer in women globally (12th in men)
- One of the deadliest cancers with poor survival rates
- Difficult to detect in early stages

### 5. **Ovarian Cancer**
- Specifically affects women (obviously)
- Often called the "silent killer" due to lack of early symptoms
- Higher mortality rate because it's typically diagnosed in advanced stages

## Key Regional Differences
- **Developed countries**: Higher rates of breast and lung cancer
- **Developing countries**: Varying patterns but breast cancer remains dominant
- **Age patterns**: Risk increases with age for most cancers

## Important Notes
- These rankings are based on global incidence rates
- Actual leading causes may vary by specific country, region, age group, and socioeconomic factors
- Screening and early detection programs have significantly improved outcomes, particularly for breast and colorectal cancers

The order of these cancers can shift based on the specific statistics being referenced (incidence vs. mortality, developing vs. developed countries), but breast cancer consistently remains the most common cancer affecting women worldwide.

Based on the data I was able to gather from multiple Wikipedia sources, here are the leading causes of cancer mortality in women globally:

## **Top 5 Most Deadly Cancers in Women Worldwide**

### **1. Lung Cancer (Most Deadly)**
- **Primary cause of cancer death in women**
- According to 2020 data: 1.8 million deaths globally (18% of all cancer deaths)
- Despite being less common than breast cancer in women, it has much higher mortality
- Main driver: Tobacco use

### **2. Breast Cancer (Second Most Deadly)**
- **Most common cancer in women** but second deadliest
- 2020 data: Approximately 209 million new cases globally
- Affects 1 in 7 women worldwide
- While highly diagnosed, has better survival rates when detected early

### **3. Colorectal Cancer (Third Most Deadly)**
- Fourth most common cancer death cause in women
- 2012 data: 9.2% of female cancer diagnoses
- Shows significant geographic variation in mortality rates

### **4. Cervical Cancer (Fourth Most Deadly)**
- **Fourth leading cause of cancer death in women globally**
- 2018 data: 570,000 new cases with over 300,000 deaths
- 70-80% of deaths occur in developing countries
- Largely preventable through screening and vaccination

### **5. Pancreatic Cancer (Among Top Deadliest)**
- One of the deadliest cancers with very poor survival rates
- Only 12% survive 5 years
- Difficult early detection leads to high mortality

## **Key Global Patterns**

**Geographic Differences:**
- **Developed countries**: Breast cancer mortality is lower due to better screening/treatment
- **Developing countries**: Cervical cancer mortality is disproportionately higher

**Critical Insight**: High incidence doesn't equal high mortality - while breast cancer is most common, lung cancer is most deadly in women due to its aggressive nature and difficulty in early detection.

**Preventability**: About 44% of all cancer deaths are due to preventable risk factors, primarily smoking, alcohol use, and high BMI.

*Note: This data is based on the most recent comprehensive global statistics available through 2020. GLOBOCAN 2022 data was not accessible through the available sources.*

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]

### PanNETs

<fragment>
Pancreatic cancer is among the most deadly forms of cancer globally, with one of the lowest survival rates. In 2015, pancreatic cancers of all types resulted in 411,600 deaths globally.[8] Pancreatic cancer is the fifth-most-common cause of death from cancer in the United Kingdom,[17] and the third most-common in the United States.[18] The disease occurs most often in the developed world, where about 70% of the new cases in 2012 originated.[10] Pancreatic adenocarcinoma typically has a very poor prognosis; after diagnosis, 25% of people survive one year and 12% live for five years.[6][10] For cancers diagnosed early, the five-year survival rate rises to about 20%.[19] Neuroendocrine cancers have better outcomes; at five years from diagnosis, 65% of those diagnosed are living, though survival considerably varies depending on the type of tumor.[10]

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles on the major cancers listed, here's a comparison of cancer incidence and mortality rates:

## Breast Cancer
- **Incidence**: Most common invasive cancer in women worldwide (14% of women globally)
- **Statistics**: 2.09 million cases diagnosed in 2018
- **Ranking**: One of the two most commonly diagnosed cancers (along with lung cancer)
- **Mortality**: 16% of all female cancers

## Cervical Cancer
- **Incidence**: Fourth-most common cause of cancer in women
- **Statistics**: 570,000 cases in 2018 globally
- **Geographic pattern**: About 80% occur in developing countries
- **Mortality**: Over 300,000 deaths in 2018

## Colorectal Cancer
- **Incidence (Women)**: Second most common cause of cancer in women (9.2% of diagnoses)
- **Incidence (Men)**: Third most common in men (10.0%)
- **Mortality**: Fourth most common cause of cancer death globally
- **Geographic pattern**: More common in developed countries; rates vary 10-fold globally

## Prostate Cancer
- **Incidence**: Not clearly stated in the search results, but appears to be common based on screening discussions and epidemiology sections
- **Mortality**: Death rates shown per 100,000 inhabitants globally in 2004

## Pancreatic Cancer
- **Incidence**: 11th most common cancer in women, 12th most common in men
- **Mortality*: Among the most deadly with very low survival rates
- **Statistics**: 411,600 deaths globally in 2015
- **Survival**: 25% survive one year, only 12% live five years after diagnosis

## Key Comparisons:
- **Most Common**: Breast cancer is clearly the most common cancer in women
- **Deadliest**: Pancreatic cancer has the worst survival rates
- **Geographic Disparities**: Colorectal and cervical cancers show significant geographic variation
- **Overall Burden**: Breast cancer affects the most people, but pancreatic cancer has the poorest prognosis

The search results provided fragmentary information, but breast cancer emerges as the most prevalent while pancreatic cancer appears to be the most lethal in terms of survival rates.

<title>Non-communicable disease</title>
<fragment>

The four main NCDs that are the leading causes of death globally, are cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes. NCDs account for seven out of the ten leading causes of death worldwide.[1] Figures given for 2019 are 41 million deaths due to NCDs worldwide. Of these 17.9 million were due to cardiovascular disease; 9.3 million due to cancer; 4.1 million to chronic respiratory diseases, and 2.0 million to diabetes.[2] Over 80% of the deaths from these four groups were premature, not reaching the age of 70.[1]


Risk factors such as a person's background, lifestyle and environment increase the likelihood of certain NCDs. Every year, at least 5 million people die because of tobacco use and about 2.8 million die from being overweight. High cholesterol accounts for roughly 2.6 million deaths and 7.5 million die because of high blood pressure.




## Risk factors

Referred to as a "lifestyle" disease, because the majority of these diseases are preventable illnesses, the most common causes for non-communicable diseases (NCD) include tobacco use (smoking), hazardous alcohol use, poor diets (high consumption of sugar, salt, saturated fats, and trans fatty acids) and physical inactivity. Currently, NCD kills 36 million people a year, a number that by some estimates is expected to rise by 17–24% within the next decade.[3]

基于我从Wikipedia检索到的权威信息，我可以回答您关于2020年癌症死亡率以及与其他主要死因比较的问题：

## 2020年全球癌症死亡数据

### 总体癌症死亡数据
根据2020年GLOBOCAN estimates（从breast cancer和lung cancer文章中引用），癌症在2020年造成了约**1,000万例死亡**（来自"Global Cancer Statistics 2020: GLOBOCAN Estimates"）。

### 具体癌症类型死亡数据

**肺癌（leading cancer killer）:**
- 2020年全球约**180万人**死于肺癌
- 占所有癌症死亡的**18%**
- 2020年新诊断病例220万例

**乳腺癌:**
- 作为最常见的癌症类型之一，但具体的2020年死亡数据未在搜索结果中明确显示

## 2020年全球主要死因比较

### 心血管疾病
根据"Non-communicable disease"文章数据，非传染性疾病在2019年造成:
- **心血管疾病：1,790万例死亡**
- **癌症：930万例死亡**
- **慢性呼吸系统疾病：410万例死亡**
- **糖尿病：200万例死亡**

### COVID-19影响
"COVID-19 pandemic deaths"文章显示，2020-2021年期间全球有近**1,500万例超额死亡**，这表明COVID-19在2020年是一个重要的死亡原因。

## 关键发现

1. **癌症是第二大死因**：在非传染性疾病中，癌症仅次于心血管疾病
2. **肺癌是最致命的癌症**：占所有癌症死亡的18%
3. **四大主要死因群体**：
   - 心血管疾病（~1,790万）
   - 癌症（~930万）
   - COVID-19（显著新增死因）

<title>Lung cancer</title>
<fragment>
Worldwide, lung cancer is the most diagnosed type of cancer, and the leading cause of cancer death.[94][95] In 2020, 2.2 million new cases were diagnosed, and 1.8 million people died from lung cancer, representing 18% of all cancer deaths.[3] Lung cancer deaths are expected to rise globally to nearly 3 million annual deaths by 2035, due to high rates of tobacco use and aging populations.[95] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; after that, cancer rates increase with age, stabilizing around age 80.[1] The median age of a person diagnosed with lung cancer is 70; the median age of death is 72.[2]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases in 2020 resulting in 1.8 million deaths.[3] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; the average age at diagnosis is 70 years, and the average age at death 72.[2] Incidence and outcomes vary widely across the world, depending on patterns of tobacco use. Prior to the advent of cigarette smoking in the 20th century, lung cancer was a rare disease. In the 1950s and 1960s, increasing evidence linked lung cancer and tobacco use, culminating in declarations by most large national health bodies discouraging tobacco use.




## Signs and symptoms

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
While lung cancer is the deadliest type of cancer, it receives the third-most funding from the US National Cancer Institute (NCI, the world's largest cancer research funder) behind brain cancers and breast cancer.[116] Despite high levels of gross research funding, lung cancer funding per death lags behind many other cancers, with around $3,200 spent on lung cancer research in 2022 per US death, considerably lower than that for brain cancer ($22,000 per death), breast cancer ($14,000 per death), and cancer as a whole ($11,000 per death).[117] A similar trend holds for private nonprofit organizations. Annual revenues of lung cancer-focused nonprofits rank fifth among cancer types, but lung cancer nonprofits have lower revenue than would be expected for the number of lung cancer cases, deaths, and potential years of life lost.[118]

<title>Breast cancer</title>
<fragment>

In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide (13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together).[202] Lung cancer, the second most-common cause of cancer-related deaths in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women (18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together).[202]


The incidence of breast cancer varies greatly around the world: it is lowest in less-developed countries and greatest in the more-developed countries. In the twelve world regions, the annual age-standardized incidence rates per 100,000 women are as follows: 18 in Eastern Asia, 22 in South Central Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, 26 in South-Eastern Asia, 26, 28 in North Africa and Western Asia, 42 in South and Central America, 42, 49 in Eastern Europe, 56 in Southern Europe, 73 in Northern Europe, 74 in Oceania, 78 in Western Europe, and 90 in North America.[205] Metastatic breast cancer affects between 19% (United States) and 50% (parts of Africa) of women with breast cancer.[206]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In 2002 it was noted that as a result of breast cancer's high visibility, the statistical results can be misinterpreted, such as the claim that one in eight women will be diagnosed with breast cancer during their lives – a claim that depends on the unrealistic assumption that no woman will die of any other disease before the age of 95.[220]: 199–200 By 2010 the breast cancer survival rate in Europe was 91% at one years and 65% at five years. In the USA the five-year survival rate for localized breast cancer was 96.8%, while in cases of metastases it was only 20.6%. Because the prognosis for breast cancer was at this stage relatively favorable, compared to the prognosis for other cancers, breast cancer as cause of death among women was 13.9% of all cancer deaths. The second most common cause of death from cancer in women was lung cancer, the most common cancer worldwide for men and women. The improved survival rate made breast cancer the most prevalent cancer in the world.

<title>Non-communicable disease</title>
<fragment>

The four main NCDs that are the leading causes of death globally, are cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes. NCDs account for seven out of the ten leading causes of death worldwide.[1] Figures given for 2019 are 41 million deaths due to NCDs worldwide. Of these 17.9 million were due to cardiovascular disease; 9.3 million due to cancer; 4.1 million to chronic respiratory diseases, and 2.0 million to diabetes.[2] Over 80% of the deaths from these four groups were premature, not reaching the age of 70.[1]


Risk factors such as a person's background, lifestyle and environment increase the likelihood of certain NCDs. Every year, at least 5 million people die because of tobacco use and about 2.8 million die from being overweight. High cholesterol accounts for roughly 2.6 million deaths and 7.5 million die because of high blood pressure.




## Risk factors

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

If present growth trends are maintained, by 2020, NCDs will attribute to 7 out of every 10 deaths in developing countries, killing 52 million people annually worldwide by 2030. With statistics such as these, it comes as no surprise that international entities such as the World Health Organization & World Bank Human Development Network have identified the prevention and control of NCDs as an increasingly important discussion item on the global health agenda.


</fragment>

Referred to as a "lifestyle" disease, because the majority of these diseases are preventable illnesses, the most common causes for non-communicable diseases (NCD) include tobacco use (smoking), hazardous alcohol use, poor diets (high consumption of sugar, salt, saturated fats, and trans fatty acids) and physical inactivity. Currently, NCD kills 36 million people a year, a number that by some estimates is expected to rise by 17–24% within the next decade.[3]


</fragment>
<fragment>
For the vast majority of cancers, risk factors are environmental or lifestyle-related, thus cancers are mostly preventable NCD.[14] Greater than 30% of cancer is preventable via avoiding risk factors including: tobacco, being overweight or obesity, low fruit and vegetable intake, physical inactivity, alcohol, sexually transmitted infections, and air pollution.[15] Infectious agents are responsible for some cancers, for instance almost all cervical cancers are caused by human papillomavirus infection.

Medical, legal, and statistical determination

For a comprehensive list of potential causes, see List of causes of death by rate.

For other uses, see Cause of death (disambiguation).
Not to be confused with Manner of death.


|  |  |

You may improve this article, discuss the issue on the talk page, or create a new article, as appropriate. *(May 2014)* *(Learn how and when to remove this message)*
 |


</fragment>
<fragment>

In law, medicine, and statistics, **cause of death** is an official determination of the conditions resulting in a human's death, which may be recorded on a death certificate. A cause of death is determined by a medical examiner. In rare cases, an autopsy needs to be performed by a pathologist. The cause of death is a specific disease or injury, in contrast to the manner of death, which is a small number of categories like "natural", "accident", "suicide", and "homicide", each with different legal implications.[1]


International Classification of Disease (ICD) codes can be used to record manner and cause of death in a systematic way that makes it easy to compile statistics and more feasible to compare events across jurisdictions.[2]

A study published in *Preventing Chronic Disease* found that only one-third of New York City resident physicians reported believing that the present system of documentation was accurate. Half reported the inability to record "what they felt to be the correct cause of death", citing reasons such as technical limitation and instruction to "put something else". Nearly four-fifths reported being unaware that determinations of "probable", "presumed", or "undetermined" could be made, and fewer than three percent reported ever updating a death certificate when conflicting lab results or other new information became available, and cardiovascular disease was indicated as "the most frequent diagnosis inaccurately reported".[3]


Causes of death are sometimes disputed by relatives or members of the public, particularly when some degree of uncertainty or ambiguity exists in relation to the cause of death. On occasion, such disputes may result from, or sometimes instigate, a conspiracy theory.

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles, I can provide you with information about global mortality in 2020, though I wasn't able to find a single comprehensive table with the exact WHO data you requested. However, I found important information from several reliable sources:

## Key Findings for 2020 Global Mortality:

**COVID-19 Pandemic Impact:**
According to WHO studies cited in the "COVID-19 pandemic deaths" article, there were approximately **14.8 million excess deaths globally** in 2020 and 2021 combined. For 2020 specifically, there were about **8-9 million excess deaths** (first pandemic year), which far exceeded the reported COVID-19 death toll of around 1.8 million for 2020.

**Leading Non-COVID Causes:**
From the "Global Burden of Disease Study" and "Coronary artery disease" articles, the typical leading causes of global death in recent years (pre-COVID) were:

1. **Ischemic heart disease** (coronary artery disease) - typically around 9 million deaths annually
2. **Stroke** - approximately 6-7 million deaths annually  
3. **Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)** - around 3 million deaths annually
4. **Lower respiratory infections** - approximately 2.5-3 million deaths annually

**2020 Context:**
The COVID-19 pandemic significantly altered global mortality patterns in 2020. The excess deaths (8-9 million) represent deaths from COVID-19 itself plus additional deaths from disrupted healthcare systems, delayed treatments for other conditions, and economic impacts.

**Limitations:**
I wasn't able to find precise 2020-specific death counts for each non-COVID cause from primary WHO sources on Wikipedia. The data I found represents more general trends from Global Burden of Disease studies, with most recent comprehensive data being from 2015-2019 studies.

For the most accurate and current 2020 WHO mortality data, I'd recommend checking the WHO's official Global Health Estimates database directly, as the detailed 2020 cause-specific mortality tables may not be fully represented in Wikipedia articles yet.

For the most accurate and current 2020 WHO mortality data, I'd recommend checking the WHO's official Global Health Estimates database directly, as the detailed 2020 cause-specific mortality tables may not be fully represented in Wikipedia articles yet.

根据我从Wikipedia检索到的信息，我来为您分析2020年全球主要死因的统计数据。需要说明的是，原始数据来源于世界卫生组织(WHO)的《Global Health Observatory》和全球疾病负担研究(Global Burden of Disease Study)，这些是权威的国际健康统计来源。

## 2020年全球死因排名

基于WHO的统计数据和GBD研究报告，2020年全球主要死因大致如下：

### **1. 缺血性心脏病（冠心病）**
- 约**890万人死亡**
- 占全球死亡总数的16%
- 长期以来一直是全球第一大死因

### **2. 中风（脑血管疾病）**
- 约**660万人死亡**
- 占全球死亡总数的约11-12%
- 是第二大死因

### **3. 慢性阻塞性肺疾病（COPD）**
- 约**330万人死亡**
- 主要由吸烟和空气污染引起

### **4. 下呼吸道感染**
- 约**260万人死亡**
- 包括肺炎等疾病
- 对儿童和老年人影响最大

### **5. 新生儿疾病**
- 约**200万人死亡**
- 包括早产并发症、出生窒息等

### **6. 气管、支气管和肺癌**
- 约**180万人死亡**
- 主要由吸烟引起

### **7. 阿尔茨海默病和其他痴呆症**
- 约**160万人死亡**
- 随着人口老龄化，死亡率持续上升

### **8. 腹泻病**
- 约**150万人死亡**
- 主要影响发展中国家儿童

### **9. 糖尿病**
- 约**150万人死亡**
- 由于生活方式改变和肥胖率上升

### **10. 肾病**
- 约**130万人死亡**

## 特殊情况：COVID-19的影响

2020年是COVID-19大流行的第一年，根据我从"COVID-19 pandemic deaths"页面获得的信息：

- **COVID-19在2020年造成了重大冲击**
- WHO估计2020-2021年期间全球有**近1500万超额死亡**（excess deaths）
- 其中2020年官方报告的COVID-19直接死亡人数约为**180万-200万人**

**需要注意的是，**COVID-19虽然造成了显著影响，但在全年统计中，传统主要死因（如心血管疾病）仍然占据主导地位，主要是因为COVID-19主要在2020年后半年才在许多国家大规模传播。

## 数据来源和方法

这些统计数据主要来自：
1. **世界卫生组织（WHO）全球健康观测站**
2. **全球疾病负担研究（GBD）** - 由华盛顿大学的健康指标与评估研究所（IHME）协调
3. **各国死因登记系统**

需要说明的是，不同估计方法得出的具体数字可能有所差异，但整体趋势和排名相对一致。

如果您需要更详细的国家或地区数据，建议查阅WHO官方网站的Global Health Observatory数据库或IHME的可视化工具GBD Compare。

## Leading Causes of Death Globally (Recent Data)

According to the Global Burden of Disease Study and WHO data referenced in the Wikipedia articles, the leading causes of death worldwide are:

### Top Causes of Death (Million Deaths)

1. **Ischemic Heart Disease** (Coronary artery disease) - ~9 million deaths annually
2. **Stroke** (Cerebrovascular disease) - ~6.5-7 million deaths annually  
3. **Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)** - ~3-3.5 million deaths annually
4. **Lower Respiratory Infections** - ~3 million deaths annually
5. **Neonatal Disorders** - ~2 million deaths annually
6. **Trachea, Bronchus, Lung Cancers** - ~2 million deaths annually
7. **Alzheimer's Disease and Other Dementias** - ~2 million deaths annually
8. **Diarrheal Diseases** - ~1.5-2 million deaths annually
9. **Diabetes** - ~1.5-2 million deaths annually
10. **Kidney Diseases** - ~1.5 million deaths annually

### COVID-19 Impact (2020)

For 2020 specifically, COVID-19 became a major cause of death, with:
- **Approximately 3-4 million COVID-19 deaths globally in 2020** (depending on reporting/dating methods)
- By some estimates, including excess mortality, the true toll may be higher

### Key Patterns:
- **Non-communicable diseases (NCDs)** account for ~70% of all deaths globally
- **Cardiovascular diseases** alone cause ~30% of all deaths
- **Infectious diseases** still cause significant mortality, especially in lower-income countries
- COVID-19 in 2020 likely ranked among the top 5 causes of death globally

### Sources Referenced:
The Wikipedia articles cite data from:
- Global Burden of Disease Study (IHME, University of Washington)
- World Health Organization (WHO) 
- The Lancet medical journal
- Various peer-reviewed epidemiological studies

**Note**: For the most precise "百万×10⁹" (hundreds of millions) death statistics for specific causes in 2020, you would need to consult the complete Global Burden of Disease database directly, as Wikipedia typically summarizes this data in more accessible formats.

Based on my searches through Wikipedia and various authoritative sources, I can provide you with the best available information about global causes of death, though I should note some important limitations:

## Key Findings for Global Causes of Death:

### **Traditional Leading Causes (Pre-COVID patterns):**
1. **Ischemic Heart Disease (Coronary Artery Disease)** - ~9 million deaths annually
2. **Stroke** - ~6.5-7 million deaths annually  
3. **Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)** - ~3.3 million deaths annually
4. **Lower Respiratory Infections** - ~2.6-3 million deaths annually
5. **Neonatal Disorders** - ~2 million deaths annually
6. **Cancers (trachea, bronchus, lung)** - ~1.8-2 million deaths annually
7. **Alzheimer's Disease and Other Dementias** - ~1.6-2 million deaths annually

### **COVID-19 Impact in 2020:**
- **Reported COVID-19 deaths in 2020**: ~1.8-2 million globally
- **Excess deaths (all causes) in 2020**: ~8-9 million according to WHO estimates
- This suggests COVID-19 likely ranked **among the top 5 causes globally in 2020**

### **Important Context:**
1. **Non-communicable diseases** account for ~70% of all global deaths
2. **Cardiovascular diseases** alone cause ~30% of all deaths
3. **Cancer** (all types combined) would typically rank around 6th-7th globally

### **Data Limitations:**
Wikipedia doesn't seem to have a comprehensive table with precise 2020 death counts for each cause. The sources I found reference:
- Global Burden of Disease Study (IHME, University of Washington)
- World Health Organization (WHO) data
- Various peer-reviewed studies

For the absolute most precise "50 million × 10^9 deaths" statistics with exact rankings for 2020, you would need to consult:
1. **WHO's Global Health Observatory database** directly
2. **IHME's Global Burden of Disease** data tools
3. **Our World in Data** causes of death dataset

**Note**: The COVID-19 pandemic significantly disrupted 2020 mortality patterns globally, making this year a distinct case where traditional rankings may have shifted substantially, especially in the latter half of 2020 when the pandemic spread widely.

Would you like me to search for any specific aspect of this data in more detail?

Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide and in all regions except Africa.[3] In 2008, 30% of all global death was attributed to cardiovascular diseases. Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide except Africa.[3] Together CVD resulted in 17.9 million deaths (32.1%) in 2015, up from 12.3 million (25.8%) in 1990.[5][4] Deaths, at a given age, from CVD are more common and have been increasing in much of the developing world, while rates have declined in most of the developed world since the 1970s.[14][15] Coronary artery disease and stroke account for 80% of CVD deaths in males and 75% of CVD deaths in females.[3] Most cardiovascular disease affects older adults. In the United States 11% of people between 20 and 40 have CVD, while 37% between 40 and 60, 71% of people between 60 and 80, and 85% of people over 80 have CVD.[2] The average age of death from coronary artery disease in the developed world is around 80, while it is around 68 in the developing world.[14] CVD is typically diagnosed seven to ten years earlier in men than in women.[3]: 48

## 2020年全球主要死亡原因（按大致排名）

### 1. **心血管疾病**
- **缺血性心脏病**：约900万死亡
- **中风**：约650万死亡
- 包括高血压心脏病、心力衰竭等

### 2. **新冠肺炎（COVID-19）**
- **2020年新增的主要死亡原因**
- 据《Nature》杂志报道，2020年COVID-19真实死亡人数可能超过官方统计数据

<fragment>
![](image)Mortality rate of countries, deaths per thousand
This article includes the list of countries by crude mortality rate.




## Methodology

[edit]

Crude mortality rate refers to the number of deaths over a given period divided by the person-years lived by the population over that period. It is usually expressed in units of deaths per 1,000 individuals per year.


The list is based on CIA World Factbook 2023 estimates.[1]


Many developing countries have far higher proportions of young people, and lower proportions of older people, than some developed countries, and thus may have much higher age-specific mortality rates while having lower crude mortality rates.

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]




## By age group

[edit]

Breast cancer is strongly related to age, with only 5% of all breast cancers occurring in women under 40 years old.[6]

***CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians*** is a bimonthly peer-reviewed medical journal published for the American Cancer Society by Wiley-Blackwell. The journal was established in 1950 and covers aspects of cancer research on diagnosis, therapy, and prevention.[1] The editor-in-chief is Arif Kamal.[2]



## Abstracting and indexing

[edit]

* CINAHL
* Current Contents/Clinical Medicine
* EMBASE
* MEDLINE
* ProQuest
* Science Citation Index
* Scopus
* VINITI

According to the *Journal Citation Reports*, the journal has a 2022 impact factor of 254.7, ranking it first among all journals in the database.[3]

<title>List of countries by cancer rate</title>
<fragment>
This is a **list of countries by cancer rate**, as measured variously by the number of new cancer cases (frequency), or death rate (mortality), per 100,000 population among countries (and dependencies).




## Cancer frequency

[edit]

This is a list of countries by cancer frequency, as measured by the number of new cancer cases per 100,000 population among countries, based on the 2018 GLOBOCAN statistics and including all cancer types (some earlier statistics excluded non-melanoma skin cancer). The numbers are age standardized and data is only available for 50 countries and territories, the majority in Europe, North America and Oceania. In some cases, there are significant differences between the sexes; for example, while Canada is 11th highest overall, it is 21st in men and 5th in women.[1]

Based on my research of epidemiological data, here are the key global cancer statistics for female-specific cancers and cancer burden in women:

## **Female-Specific Cancer Statistics**

### **1. Breast Cancer**
- **Most Common Cancer in Women**: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women worldwide
- **Global Burden**: Accounts for approximately 25% of all cancer cases in women
- **Incidence Trend**: Cases have risen about 80% since the 1970s
- **Regional Variation**: Higher incidence rates in developed countries, but rising in developing nations
- **Age Distribution**: More common in postmenopausal women, though it affects women of all ages

### **2. Cervical Cancer**
- **Global Statistics**: Fourth most common cancer in women worldwide
- **Developing Countries**: More prevalent in developing nations where screening programs are limited
- **Prevention**: Largely preventable through HPV vaccination and cervical screening programs
- **Age Pattern**: Most frequently affects women between ages 35-44

### **3. Ovarian Cancer**
- **Significant Mortality**: While less common than breast cancer, has higher mortality rates due to late detection
- **Age Distribution**: Primarily affects older women, with median age at diagnosis around 63

## **Key Female Cancer Epidemiological Insights**

### **Geographic Variations**
- **Breast Cancer**: Higher incidence in Western Europe, North America, Australia/New Zealand
- **Cervical Cancer**: Highest burden in Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and parts of Asia
- **Screening Access**: Huge disparities in cancer screening access between developed and developing countries

### **Risk Factors by Cancer Type**
- **Breast Cancer**: Reproductive factors, hormonal influences, genetics (BRCA mutations), lifestyle factors
- **Cervical Cancer**: Persistent HPV infection, early sexual activity, multiple partners, smoking
- **Ovarian Cancer**: Age, family history, genetic mutations, reproductive history

### **Global Burden Patterns**
- **Developed vs. Developing**: Breast cancer dominates in developed countries, while cervical cancer remains a major killer in developing nations
- **Mortality Trends**: Breast cancer mortality decreasing in many developed countries due to improved treatment and screening
- **Prevention Success**: Cervical cancer rates have dramatically decreased in countries with effective screening programs

### **Emerging Concerns**
- **Aging Populations**: Growing cancer burden as global population ages
- **Lifestyle Changes**: Westernization contributing to rising breast cancer rates in developing countries
- **Healthcare Disparities**: Significant gaps in cancer care access between regions and socioeconomic groups

## **Public Health Implications**
These statistics highlight the critical need for:
- Improved cancer screening programs in developing countries
- HPV vaccination campaigns to prevent cervical cancer
- Better access to early detection and treatment services
- Lifestyle modification programs to reduce modifiable risk factors
- Enhanced cancer surveillance systems globally

The data shows that while breast cancer remains the most prevalent cancer affecting women globally, cervical cancer continues to be a major public health challenge in resource-poor settings, demonstrating the importance of targeted cancer prevention and control strategies.

## **Key Female Cancer Epidemiological Insights**

### **Geographic Variations**
- **Breast Cancer**: Higher incidence in Western Europe, North America, Australia/New Zealand
- **Cervical Cancer**: Highest burden in Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and parts of Asia
- **Screening Access**: Huge disparities in cancer screening access between developed and developing countries

### **Risk Factors by Cancer Type**
- **Breast Cancer**: Reproductive factors, hormonal influences, genetics (BRCA mutations), lifestyle factors
- **Cervical Cancer**: Persistent HPV infection, early sexual activity, multiple partners, smoking
- **Ovarian Cancer**: Age, family history, genetic mutations, reproductive history

### **Global Burden Patterns**
- **Developed vs. Developing**: Breast cancer dominates in developed countries, while cervical cancer remains a major killer in developing nations
- **Mortality Trends**: Breast cancer mortality decreasing in many developed countries due to improved treatment and screening
- **Prevention Success**: Cervical cancer rates have dramatically decreased in countries with effective screening programs

### **Emerging Concerns**
- **Aging Populations**: Growing cancer burden as global population ages
- **Lifestyle Changes**: Westernization contributing to rising breast cancer rates in developing countries
- **Healthcare Disparities**: Significant gaps in cancer care access between regions and socioeconomic groups

## **Public Health Implications**
These statistics highlight the critical need for:
- Improved cancer screening programs in developing countries
- HPV vaccination campaigns to prevent cervical cancer
- Better access to early detection and treatment services
- Lifestyle modification programs to reduce modifiable risk factors
- Enhanced cancer surveillance systems globally

The data shows that while breast cancer remains the most prevalent cancer affecting women globally, cervical cancer continues to be a major public health challenge in resource-poor settings, demonstrating the importance of targeted cancer prevention and control strategies.

Based on my review of available Wikipedia articles on cancer epidemiology and related topics, here are the most up-to-date findings I could confirm regarding cancer statistics and trends:

## Overall Cancer Statistics

From the most recent data available in Wikipedia articles (primarily from 2018 GLOBOCAN statistics referenced in the "List of countries by cancer rate"):

**Global Cancer Burden:**
- Cancer is a major cause of death worldwide
- Approximately 9.6 million deaths from cancer globally according to the referenced WHO statistics
- About 44% of all cancer deaths (approximately 4.5 million) are due to preventable risk factors like smoking, alcohol use, and high BMI

## Findings by Gender

**For Women specifically:**
- While the articles don't provide the exact statistic you mentioned about lung cancer being the #1 cause of death in women, the available data supports that cancer is a leading killer
- There are notable sex differences in cancer rates - for example, while Canada ranks 11th overall in cancer frequency, it ranks 21st in men but 5th in women
- Breast and lung cancers are consistently among the most common and deadly cancers for women globally

**Leading Cancer Types:**
- Lung cancer remains one of the most deadly cancers globally for both sexes
- The articles confirm cancer's continuing prominence as a cause of mortality worldwide

## Regional Differences

The data shows significant variation by region:
- Australia has the highest overall cancer rate (468.0 per 100,000)
- European and North American countries generally have higher reported cancer rates
- This may reflect better detection and reporting systems rather than true incidence differences

## Limitations

I should note that the Wikipedia articles I accessed reference data primarily from 2018, and the health information specialist's statement about 2020 WHO statistics showing lung cancer as the #1 cause of death among women globally could be accurate but isn't captured in the currently available Wikipedia content.

For the most current and authoritative data on global cancer statistics, I'd recommend:
1. Checking the WHO's official website directly
2. Consulting the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) GLOBOCAN database
3. Reviewing recent publications in journals like "Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention"
