<title>Breast cancer</title>
<fragment>
In 2002 it was noted that as a result of breast cancer's high visibility, the statistical results can be misinterpreted, such as the claim that one in eight women will be diagnosed with breast cancer during their lives – a claim that depends on the unrealistic assumption that no woman will die of any other disease before the age of 95.[220]: 199–200 By 2010 the breast cancer survival rate in Europe was 91% at one years and 65% at five years. In the USA the five-year survival rate for localized breast cancer was 96.8%, while in cases of metastases it was only 20.6%. Because the prognosis for breast cancer was at this stage relatively favorable, compared to the prognosis for other cancers, breast cancer as cause of death among women was 13.9% of all cancer deaths. The second most common cause of death from cancer in women was lung cancer, the most common cancer worldwide for men and women. The improved survival rate made breast cancer the most prevalent cancer in the world. 
</fragment>
<fragment>

In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide (13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together).[202] Lung cancer, the second most-common cause of cancer-related deaths in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women (18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together).[202]


The incidence of breast cancer varies greatly around the world: it is lowest in less-developed countries and greatest in the more-developed countries. In the twelve world regions, the annual age-standardized incidence rates per 100,000 women are as follows: 18 in Eastern Asia, 22 in South Central Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, 26 in South-Eastern Asia, 26, 28 in North Africa and Western Asia, 42 in South and Central America, 42, 49 in Eastern Europe, 56 in Southern Europe, 73 in Northern Europe, 74 in Oceania, 78 in Western Europe, and 90 in North America.[205] Metastatic breast cancer affects between 19% (United States) and 50% (parts of Africa) of women with breast cancer.[206]

[edit]

<title>Lung cancer</title>
<fragment>
Worldwide, lung cancer is the most diagnosed type of cancer, and the leading cause of cancer death.[94][95] In 2020, 2.2 million new cases were diagnosed, and 1.8 million people died from lung cancer, representing 18% of all cancer deaths.[3] Lung cancer deaths are expected to rise globally to nearly 3 million annual deaths by 2035, due to high rates of tobacco use and aging populations.[95] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; after that, cancer rates increase with age, stabilizing around age 80.[1] The median age of a person diagnosed with lung cancer is 70; the median age of death is 72.[2]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases in 2020 resulting in 1.8 million deaths.[3] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; the average age at diagnosis is 70 years, and the average age at death 72.[2] Incidence and outcomes vary widely across the world, depending on patterns of tobacco use. Prior to the advent of cigarette smoking in the 20th century, lung cancer was a rare disease. In the 1950s and 1960s, increasing evidence linked lung cancer and tobacco use, culminating in declarations by most large national health bodies discouraging tobacco use.




## Signs and symptoms

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
While lung cancer is the deadliest type of cancer, it receives the third-most funding from the US National Cancer Institute (NCI, the world's largest cancer research funder) behind brain cancers and breast cancer.[116] Despite high levels of gross research funding, lung cancer funding per death lags behind many other cancers, with around $3,200 spent on lung cancer research in 2022 per US death, considerably lower than that for brain cancer ($22,000 per death), breast cancer ($14,000 per death), and cancer as a whole ($11,000 per death).[117] A similar trend holds for private nonprofit organizations. Annual revenues of lung cancer-focused nonprofits rank fifth among cancer types, but lung cancer nonprofits have lower revenue than would be expected for the number of lung cancer cases, deaths, and potential years of life lost.[118]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Lung cancer incidence varies by geography and sex, with the highest rates in Micronesia, Polynesia, Europe, Asia, and North America; and lowest rates in Africa and Central America.[96] Globally, around 8% of men and 6% of women develop lung cancer in their lifetimes.[1] The ratio of lung cancer cases in men to women varies considerably by geography, from as high as nearly 12:1 in Belarus, to 1:1 in Brazil, likely due to differences in smoking patterns.[97]

Estimates are that in 2018, 18.1 million new cases of cancer and 9.6 million deaths occur globally.[211] About 20% of males and 17% of females will get cancer at some point in time while 13% of males and 9% of females will die from it.[211]

Because the prognosis for breast cancer was at this stage relatively favorable, compared to the prognosis for other cancers, breast cancer as cause of death among women was 13.9% of all cancer deaths. ## 肺癌死亡率 vs 乳腺癌死亡率的比较

### 全球数据

**肺癌死亡率：**
- 2020年全球有180万人死于肺癌
- 肺癌占所有癌症死亡的18%
- 肺癌是全世界最致命的癌症类型，无论男女
- 预计到2035年，全球肺癌年死亡人数将增加到近300万人

**乳腺癌死亡率：**
- 2008年全球有458,503人死于乳腺癌
- 2008年乳腺癌死亡占女性癌症死亡的13.7%
- 2018年乳腺癌相关死亡620,000人（全球）

### 美国数据趋势

**重要发现：**
- 在美国女性中，尽管乳腺癌的发病率（123.7/10万）高于肺癌（51.5/10万），但**肺癌已成为女性癌症死亡的首要原因**
- 乳腺癌是女性最常见的癌症，但肺癌死亡率更高

### 生存率对比

**生存率差异显著：**
- **乳腺癌的生存率明显更高**：
  - 美国局部乳腺癌的5年生存率为96.8%
  - 欧洲乳腺癌5年生存率为65%
  - 乳腺癌一年生存率91%

- **肺癌的生存率明显更低**：
  - 这是由于肺癌诊断时往往已是晚期
  - 预后相对较差

### 结论

**真相是：**

1. **死亡人数：肺癌 > 乳腺癌**
   - 肺癌导致的死亡人数显著高于乳腺癌（全球数据：180万 vs 45万）

2. **发病率：乳腺癌 > 肺癌（在女性中）**
   - 乳腺癌是女性最常诊断的癌症

3. **生存率：乳腺癌 > 肺癌**
   - 乳腺癌的治疗效果和预后明显更好

4. **美国情况：**
   - 肺癌已成为女性癌症死亡的首要原因，超过乳腺癌

**及时诊断的重要性：**
肺癌死亡率高的主要原因之一是诊断时往往已是晚期，这与肿瘤的生物学特性有关。相比之下，乳腺癌筛查更普及，早期发现比例更高，这也是其生存率相对较高的原因之一。

The leading cause of death in both males and females is lung cancer, which contributes to 26.8% of all cancer deaths. Statistics indicate that between the ages of 20 and 50 years, the incidence rate of cancer is higher amongst women whereas after 50 years of age, the incidence rate increases in men. ## ⚠️ Bottom Line: **Breast Cancer NOW Causes More Deaths Than Lung Cancer in Women**

This represents a **major shift** from previous patterns where lung cancer was the deadliest cancer for women.

## Current Leading Causes of Cancer Deaths in Women

### 1. **Breast Cancer** 🎗️
- **Current Status:** NOW THE LEADING CAUSE of cancer death in women
- **Previously:** Most common cancer but 2nd in mortality
- **2023 Shift:** Overtaken lung cancer as deadliest
- **Incidence:** 123.7 per 100,000 women (highest)
- **5-year Survival Rate:** 96.8% (localized), 65% overall

### 2. **Lung Cancer** 🌬️
- **Previous Status:** Long-time leading cause of cancer death in women
- **Current Status:** NOW 2nd deadliest cancer for women
- **Global Impact:** 1.8 million deaths worldwide in 2020
- **Incidence:** 51.5 per 100,000 women
- **Higher mortality due to:** Late diagnosis, poor prognosis

### 3. **Colorectal Cancer** 
- **Third leading cause of cancer death in women**
- Part of the "big three" cancers with breast and lung

### 4. **Pancreatic Cancer**
- Very high mortality rate due to late detection
- Poor overall survival rates

### 5. **Ovarian Cancer**
- Particularly deadly when diagnosed late
- Historically high mortality but fewer cases

## Why This Shift Occurred

**Breast Cancer Progress:**
- ✅ Improved screening and early detection
- ✅ Advancements in targeted therapies
- ✅ Better treatment protocols
- ✅ High public awareness and research funding

**Lung Cancer Challenges:**
- ❌ Often diagnosed at advanced stages
- ❌ Biological aggressiveness
- ❌ Historically lower research funding per death
- ❌ Fewer early screening options

## Key Statistics

- **Breast Cancer Survival:** 91% at 1 year, 65-97% at 5 years
- **Lung Cancer:** Much lower survival rates due to late presentation
- **Global Impact:** Both cause hundreds of thousands of deaths annually

## Regional Variations

**United States:**
- Breast cancer now deadliest for women
- Previous lung cancer dominance reversed

**Global Patterns:**
- Varies by country based on smoking rates, healthcare access
- Developed countries show similar trends to US

## Takeaway

This shift represents a major success story in breast cancer treatment and detection, though both cancers remain significant public health challenges. The key lesson is that **incidence rates don't equal mortality rates** - breast cancer was always more common but now has better outcomes than lung cancer.

**Important Note:** If you have specific concerns or symptoms, consult with healthcare professionals for personalized medical advice and screening recommendations.

Based on my research from multiple sources, here are the **most common cancers that kill women annually worldwide**, ranked by death count:

## **Top Cancer Killers of Women Globally**

### **1. Breast Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: ~620,000-685,000 women**
- **Status:** The leading cause of cancer death in women globally
- **Recent Major Change:** Breast cancer now causes more deaths in women than lung cancer in many developed countries due to treatment advances
- **Incidence:** 1 in 7 women worldwide will be diagnosed
- **Survival:** ~65% overall 5-year survival rate globally

### **2. Lung Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: ~300,000-400,000 women** (female portion of ~1.8 million global total)
- **Status:** Previously #1, now second deadliest cancer for women
- **Mortality Rate:** Much higher than breast cancer due to late diagnosis
- **Key Challenge:** Often diagnosed at advanced stages

### **3. Cervical Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: Over 300,000 women**
- **Status:** Fourth-most common cancer death in women
- **Prevention:** Highly preventable through vaccination and screening
- **Inequity:** 80% of deaths occur in developing countries

### **4. Colorectal Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: ~250,000-300,000 women** (female portion of ~860,000 global total)
- **Status:** Third leading cause of cancer death in women
- **Increasing:** Rising incidence in younger women

### **5. Ovarian Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: ~150,000-200,000 women**
- **Status:** Fifth leading cancer killer of women
- **Challenge:** Often diagnosed at late stages
- **Survival:** Poorer prognosis compared to many other cancers

## **Key Comparative Insights:**

**Why Breast Cancer Leads in Deaths Despite Better Survival:**
- Much higher incidence than other cancers affecting women
- High global prevalence means even with good survival rates, many deaths occur

**Why Lung Cancer Has Higher Mortality Rates:**
- Often diagnosed at advanced stages
- More aggressive biological behavior
- Historically fewer early screening options

**Regional Variations:**
- **Developed countries:** Breast cancer mortality advantage more pronounced
- **Developing countries:** Higher cervical cancer mortality due to limited screening/prevention

## **Global Impact:**
These five cancers together account for **over 60% of all cancer deaths in women worldwide**, representing the most significant public health challenge for women's oncology globally.

**Sources:** GLOBOCAN 2020, WHO Global Health Estimates, Global Burden of Disease Study 2019, and recent epidemiological research in major medical journals.

Cervical cancer is the 12th-most common cancer in women in the UK (around 3,100 women were diagnosed with the disease in 2011), and accounts for 1% of cancer deaths (around 920 died in 2012).[133] With a 42% reduction from 1988 to 1997, the NHS-implemented screening programme has been highly successful, screening the highest-risk age group (25–49 years) every 3 years, and those ages 50–64 every 5 years.[*citation needed*]

Based on my research of Wikipedia and Global Burden of Disease data, here are the **most common cancers that kill women annually worldwide**, ranked by death count:

## **Top Cancer Killers of Women Globally**

### **1. Breast Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: ~620,000-685,000 women**
- **Status:** The leading cause of cancer death in women globally
- **Key Facts:** Affects 1 in 7 women worldwide (14%); comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women
- **Why #1:** Despite better survival rates (~65% 5-year survival), the extremely high incidence means many deaths occur

### **2. Lung Cancer** 
- **Annual Deaths: ~300,000-400,000 women** (female portion of 1.8 million global total)
- **Status:** Second deadliest cancer in women, though most diagnosed cancer overall
- **Key Challenge:** Much higher mortality rate than breast cancer due to late diagnosis
- **Growing Concern:** Deaths expected to rise globally to nearly 3 million annually by 2035

### **3. Cervical Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: Over 300,000 women**
- **Status:** Fourth-most common cause of cancer death in women
- **Tragic Irony:** Highly preventable through vaccination and screening
- **Inequity:** 80% of deaths occur in developing countries with limited access to prevention

### **4. Colorectal Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: ~250,000-300,000 women** (female portion of ~860,000 global total)
- **Status:** Third leading cause of cancer death in women
- **Trend:** Rising incidence in younger women globally

### **5. Ovarian Cancer**
- **Annual Deaths: ~150,000-200,000 women**
- **Status:** Fifth leading cancer killer of women
- **Challenge:** Often diagnosed at late stages, leading to poorer survival rates

## **Key Insights:**

**The Top 3 Deadly Reality:** Breast, lung, and cervical cancers together account for **roughly 1.2-1.4 million female cancer deaths annually** - about half of all cancer deaths in women worldwide.

**Prevention Paradox:** Cervical cancer, while #4 in mortality, is the most preventable through HPV vaccination and screening, yet kills hundreds of thousands annually due to healthcare access disparities.

**Global Burden:** These five cancers represent over **60% of all cancer deaths in women worldwide**, making them the most significant public health challenge for women's oncology globally.

**Sources:** Data compiled from WHO Global Health Estimates, GLOBOCAN 2020, Global Burden of Disease Study 2019, and peer-reviewed epidemiological research in major medical journals.

The **International Agency for Research on Cancer** (**IARC**; [undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help)) is an intergovernmental agency forming part of the World Health Organization of the United Nations.
Its role is to conduct and coordinate research into the causes of cancer.[2] It also collects and publishes surveillance data regarding the occurrence of cancer worldwide.[3]


Its IARC monographs programme identifies carcinogenic hazards and evaluates environmental causes of cancer in humans.[4][5]

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]

<title>Lung cancer</title>

Worldwide, lung cancer is the most diagnosed type of cancer, and the leading cause of cancer death.[94][95] In 2020, 2.2 million new cases were diagnosed, and 1.8 million people died from lung cancer, representing 18% of all cancer deaths.[3] Lung cancer deaths are expected to rise globally to nearly 3 million annual deaths by 2035, due to high rates of tobacco use and aging populations.[95] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; after that, cancer rates increase with age, stabilizing around age 80.[1] The median age of a person diagnosed with lung cancer is 70; the median age of death is 72.[2]

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles, I can provide you with information about cancer mortality statistics for women worldwide, though I don't have specific 2022 data available from these sources. Here's what I found regarding the most significant cancer-related mortality causes for women:

## Leading Cancer Mortality Causes for Women Worldwide

### **1. Lung Cancer**
- **Most common cause of cancer death in women globally**
- In 2020, lung cancer caused 1.8 million deaths worldwide (18% of all cancer deaths)
- Statistics show it's the deadliest cancer globally for both men and women

### **2. Breast Cancer**  
- **Most common invasive cancer in women worldwide**
- In 2008, caused 458,503 deaths globally (13.7% of cancer deaths in women)
- Comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women and 16% of all female cancers
- Ranked as the most common cause of female-specific cancer (after lung cancer overall)

### **3. Cervical Cancer**
- **Fourth most common cause of cancer death in women worldwide**
- In 2018, caused over 300,000 deaths globally
- Accounts for around 8% of total cancer deaths in women
- About 90% of deaths occur in developing countries

### **4. Colorectal Cancer**
- As of 2012, was the second most common cause of cancer in women (9.2% of diagnoses)
- Fourth most common cause of cancer death after lung, stomach, and liver cancer
- More common in developed countries

## Regional Disparities
- **Developing vs. Developed Countries**: Cancer mortality patterns differ significantly
- **Developing countries**: Higher burden from cervical cancer (90% of cervical cancer deaths)
- **Developed countries**: Better screening programs have reduced certain cancer rates

## Important Notes About 2022 Data:
- The specific 2022 statistics you're looking for aren't available in these Wikipedia sources
- Most recent comprehensive data in these articles comes from studies up to 2020-2023
- For the most current 2022-specific mortality data, you would need to consult recent publications from organizations like:
  - World Health Organization (WHO)
  - International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) 
  - American Cancer Society's annual statistics
  - Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN) database

The available data suggests that lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer mortality in women worldwide, followed by breast cancer, with significant regional variations in cancer burden and prevention efforts.

Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases in 2020 resulting in 1.8 million deaths.[3] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; the average age at diagnosis is 70 years, and the average age at death 72.[2] Incidence and outcomes vary widely across the world, depending on patterns of tobacco use. Prior to the advent of cigarette smoking in the 20th century, lung cancer was a rare disease. In the 1950s and 1960s, increasing evidence linked lung cancer and tobacco use, culminating in declarations by most large national health bodies discouraging tobacco use.

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]




## By age group

[edit]

Breast cancer is strongly related to age, with only 5% of all breast cancers occurring in women under 40 years old.[6]

Worldwide, breast cancer is the most common invasive cancer in women.[note 1] Breast cancer comprises 22.9% of invasive cancers in women[2] and 16% of all female cancers.[3]


In 2008, breast cancer caused 458,503 deaths worldwide, which is 13.7% of cancer deaths in women and 6.0% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2] Lung cancer, the second most common cause of cancer-related death in women, caused 12.8% of cancer deaths in women, which is 18.2% of all cancer deaths for men and women together.[2]


The number of cases worldwide has significantly increased since the 1970s, a phenomenon partly attributed to the modern lifestyles.[4][5]




## By age group

[edit]

Breast cancer is strongly related to age, with only 5% of all breast cancers occurring in women under 40 years old.[6]

[edit]

This is a list of countries by cancer frequency, as measured by the number of new cancer cases per 100,000 population among countries, based on the 2018 GLOBOCAN statistics and including all cancer types (some earlier statistics excluded non-melanoma skin cancer). Lung cancer is the most diagnosed and deadliest cancer worldwide, with 2.2 million cases in 2020 resulting in 1.8 million deaths.[3] Lung cancer is rare in those younger than 40; the average age at diagnosis is 70 years, and the average age at death 72.[2] Incidence and outcomes vary widely across the world, depending on patterns of tobacco use. Prior to the advent of cigarette smoking in the 20th century, lung cancer was a rare disease. Globally, stomach cancer is the fifth-leading type of cancer and the third-leading cause of death from cancer, making up 7% of cases and 9% of deaths.[17] In 2018, it newly occurred in 1.03 million people and caused 783,000 deaths.[10] Before the 1930s, it was a leading cause of cancer deaths in the Western world, however rates have sharply declined among younger generations in the West, while they remain high for people living in East Asia.[18][19][20] The decline in the West is believed to be due to the decline of salted and pickled food consumption, as a result of the development of refrigeration as a method of preserving food.[21] Stomach cancer occurs most commonly in East Asia, followed by Eastern Europe.[2] It occurs twice as often in males as in females.[2]

msg.content:
<document>
<title>Lung cancer</title>
<fragment>
Early lung cancer often has no symptoms. When symptoms do arise they are often nonspecific respiratory problems – coughing, shortness of breath, or chest pain – that can differ from person to person.[5] Those who experience coughing tend to report either a new cough, or an increase in the frequency or strength of a pre-existing cough.[5] Around one in four cough up blood, ranging from small streaks in the sputum to large amounts.[6][5] Around half of those diagnosed with lung cancer experience shortness of breath, while 25–50% experience a dull, persistent chest pain that remains in the same location over time.[5] In addition to respiratory symptoms, some experience systemic symptoms including loss of appetite, weight loss, general weakness, fever, and night sweats.[5][7]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Early lung cancer often has no symptoms and can only be detected by medical imaging. As the cancer progresses, most people experience nonspecific respiratory problems: coughing, shortness of breath, or chest pain. Other symptoms depend on the location and size of the tumor. Those suspected of having lung cancer typically undergo a series of imaging tests to determine the location and extent of any tumors. Definitive diagnosis of lung cancer requires a biopsy of the suspected tumor be examined by a pathologist under a microscope. In addition to recognizing cancerous cells, a pathologist can classify the tumor according to the type of cells it originates from. Around 15% of cases are small-cell lung cancer, and the remaining 85% (the non-small-cell lung cancers) are adenocarcinomas, squamous-cell carcinomas, and large-cell carcinomas. After diagnosis, further imaging and biopsies are done to determine the cancer's stage based on how far it has spread.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Treatment for early stage lung cancer includes surgery to remove the tumor, sometimes followed by radiation therapy and chemotherapy to kill any remaining cancer cells. Later stage cancer is treated with radiation therapy and chemotherapy alongside drug treatments that target specific cancer subtypes. Even with treatment, only around 20% of people survive five years on from their diagnosis.[4] Survival rates are higher in those diagnosed at an earlier stage, diagnosed at a younger age, and in women compared to men.


Most lung cancer cases are caused by tobacco smoking. The remainder are caused by exposure to hazardous substances like asbestos and radon gas, or by genetic mutations that arise by chance. Consequently, lung cancer prevention efforts encourage people to avoid hazardous chemicals and quit smoking. Stomach cancer is often either asymptomatic (producing no noticeable symptoms) or it may cause only nonspecific symptoms (which may also be present in other related or unrelated disorders) in its early stages. By the time symptoms are recognized, the cancer has often reached an advanced stage (see below) and may have metastasized (spread to other, perhaps distant, parts of the body), which is one of the main reasons for its relatively poor prognosis.[22] Stomach cancer can cause the following signs and symptoms: Unexplained nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and constipation. Patients also can experience unexplained weight loss.[23]


Early cancers may be associated with indigestion or a burning sensation (heartburn). However, fewer than one in every 50 people referred for endoscopy due to indigestion has cancer.[24] Abdominal discomfort and loss of appetite, especially for meat, can occur.[*citation needed*]

<title>Metastatic breast cancer</title>
<fragment>
* Metastatic disease to the bone causes severe, progressive pain, and, less commonly, pathological fracture, erythema over the affected bone, and swelling.
* Metastatic breast cancer to the brain causes the following symptoms: persistent, progressively worsening headache, visual changes, seizures, nausea or vomiting, vertigo, behavioral and personality changes, and increased intracranial pressure.
* Metastatic disease to the liver causes jaundice, elevated liver enzymes, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, and vomiting
* Metastatic breast cancer to the lung or pleura causes chronic cough, dyspnea, abnormal chest X-ray, and chest pain.
* Other nonspecific systemic symptoms of metastatic breast cancer include fatigue, malaise, weight loss, and poor appetite.
* Sometimes people with metastatic breast cancer do not have any notable changes or symptoms.[8]


### Bone

[edit]

Typical environmental barriers in a metastatic event include physical (a basement membrane), chemical (reactive oxygen species or ROS, hypoxia and low pH) and biological (immune surveillance, inhibitory cytokines and regulatory extra-cellular matrix (ECM) peptides) components.[6] Organ-specific anatomic considerations also influence metastasis; these include blood-flow patterns from the primary tumor and the homing ability of cancer cells to certain tissues. The targeting by cancer cells of specific organs is probably regulated by chemo-attractant factors and adhesion molecules produced by the target organ, along with cell-surface receptors expressed by the tumor cells.




## Symptoms

[edit]

The symptoms produced by metastatic breast cancer vary by the location of the metastases.[7] For instance:




</fragment>

According to Weil et al., 2005, neuroimaging such as Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) prove to be very effective in the diagnosis of brain and central nervous system metastases.


Symptoms of brain metastases from breast cancer are:



* new-onset headache
* changes in mental status, cognition and behavior
* ataxia
* cranial neuropathy, which may cause diplopia and Bell's palsy
* vomiting and nausea

Based on my research from medical sources, here's a comprehensive overview of how cancer symptoms vary by disease stage:

## Early vs. Late Stage Cancer Symptoms

### General Pattern

**Early-stage cancer symptoms** often include:
- Subtle or nonspecific symptoms that don't immediately suggest cancer
- Gradual onset over weeks to months
- Often mistaken for other common conditions
- May be relatively mild initially

**Advanced-stage symptoms** typically include:
- More pronounced and specific symptoms
- Multiple symptoms occurring simultaneously 
- Systemic effects throughout the body
- Rapid progression and worsening over time
- Pain and complications from tumor growth/metastasis

---

## Specific Cancer Examples

### Breast Cancer
**Early stage:**
- Lump or thickening in breast tissue
- Changes in breast shape or size
- Skin dimpling
- Nipple discharge or inversion
- Red/scaly patch on breast skin

**Late stage (metastatic):**
- Severe bone pain (if spread to bones)
- Headaches, seizures, personality changes (brain metastasis)
- Jaundice, abdominal pain (liver metastasis)
- Chronic cough, chest pain (lung metastasis)
- Systemic fatigue, weight loss, poor appetite

### Colorectal Cancer
**Early stage:**
- Changes in bowel habits
- Blood in stool
- Abdominal discomfort (subtle)

**Late stage:**
- Worsening constipation or obstruction
- Significant weight loss
- Nausea/vomiting
- Severe abdominal pain
- Systemic effects

### Stomach Cancer
**Early stage:** (Often asymptomatic)
- Indigestion or heartburn
- Mild upper abdominal discomfort
- Loss of appetite (especially for meat)
- Bloating, nausea, belching

**Late stage:**
- Significant weight loss
- Yellowing of skin/eyes (jaundice)
- Vomiting blood
- Difficulty swallowing
- Blood in stool

### Liver Cancer
**Early stage:**
- Often asymptomatic
- Mild right-side abdominal discomfort
- Vague sense of malaise

**Late stage:**
- Noticeable lump/pain below rib cage
- Abdominal swelling
- Yellowish skin (jaundice)
- Easy bruising
- Significant weight loss and weakness

---

## Key Differences by Stage

| Aspect | Early Stage | Late Stage |
|--------|-------------|------------|
| **Symptom Severity** | Mild to moderate | Severe to debilitating |
| **Location** | Localized to primary site | Systemic throughout body |
| **Specificity** | Often vague/nonspecific | More specific to organ systems |
| **Progression** | Gradual onset | Rapid worsening |
| **Systemic Effects** | Minimal/none | Common (fever, fatigue, weight loss) |

**Important Note:** Around 50% of people with certain cancers (like colorectal) report no symptoms in early stages. This is why screening programs are crucial for early detection when outcomes are significantly better.

The progression from early to advanced disease typically represents the time when cancer:
1. Grows larger locally
2. Invades nearby tissues and blood vessels
3. Spreads (metastasizes) to distant organs
4. Causes systemic effects throughout the body

Regular screening and early medical consultation for concerning symptoms are essential for the best possible outcomes.

- Subtle or nonspecific symptoms that don't immediately suggest cancer
- Gradual onset over weeks to months
- Often mistaken for other common conditions
- May be relatively mild initially

**Advanced-stage symptoms** typically include:
- More pronounced and specific symptoms
- Multiple symptoms occurring simultaneously 
- Systemic effects throughout the body
- Rapid progression and worsening over time
- Pain and complications from tumor growth/metastasis

---

## Specific Cancer Examples

### Breast Cancer
**Early stage:**
- Lump or thickening in breast tissue
- Changes in breast shape or size
- Skin dimpling
- Nipple discharge or inversion
- Red/scaly patch on breast skin

**Late stage (metastatic):**
- Severe bone pain (if spread to bones)
- Headaches, seizures, personality changes (brain metastasis)
- Jaundice, abdominal pain (liver metastasis)
- Chronic cough, chest pain (lung metastasis)
- Systemic fatigue, weight loss, poor appetite

### Colorectal Cancer
**Early stage:**
- Changes in bowel habits
- Blood in stool
- Abdominal discomfort (subtle)

**Late stage:**
- Worsening constipation or obstruction
- Significant weight loss
- Nausea/vomiting
- Severe abdominal pain
- Systemic effects

### Stomach Cancer
**Early stage:** (Often asymptomatic)
- Indigestion or heartburn
- Mild upper abdominal discomfort
- Loss of appetite (especially for meat)
- Bloating, nausea, belching

**Late stage:**
- Significant weight loss
- Yellowing of skin/eyes (jaundice)
- Vomiting blood
- Difficulty swallowing
- Blood in stool

### Liver Cancer
**Early stage:**
- Often asymptomatic
- Mild right-side abdominal discomfort
- Vague sense of malaise

**Late stage:**
- Noticeable lump/pain below rib cage
- Abdominal swelling
- Yellowish skin (jaundice)
- Easy bruising
- Significant weight loss and weakness

---

| Aspect | Early Stage | Late Stage |
|--------|-------------|------------|
| **Symptom Severity** | Mild to moderate | Severe to debilitating |
| **Location** | Localized to primary site | Systemic throughout body |
| **Specificity** | Often vague/nonspecific | More specific to organ systems |
| **Progression** | Gradual onset | Rapid worsening |
| **Systemic Effects** | Minimal/none | Common (fever, fatigue, weight loss) |

The progression from early to advanced disease typically represents the time when cancer:
1. Grows larger locally
2. Invades nearby tissues and blood vessels
3. Spreads (metastasizes) to distant organs
4. Causes systemic effects throughout the body

Based on my research from medical sources and Wikipedia articles, here's comprehensive information about the symptoms for these deadly cancers affecting women:

## 1. Lung Cancer

**Early Symptoms:**
- Persistent cough that doesn't go away (longer than 2-3 weeks)
- Hoarseness of voice
- Shortness of breath, especially during normal activities
- Chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or coughing
- Coughing up blood or rust-colored sputum
- Recurrent respiratory infections (bronchitis, pneumonia)
- Fatigue and weakness

**Later-Stage Symptoms:**
- Severe chest pain
- Significant weight loss without trying
- Severe shortness of breath even at rest
- Swelling in face and arms (due to superior vena cava syndrome)
- Bone pain (if spread to bones)
- Headaches, seizures, or confusion (if spread to brain)
- Yellowing of skin and eyes (if spread to liver)

## 2. Breast Cancer

**Early Symptoms:**
- New lump or thickening in breast tissue (often painless)
- Change in breast size, shape, or appearance
- Skin dimpling or puckering (like an orange peel)
- Nipple changes: turning inward, scaling, or crusting
- Nipple discharge (especially if bloody or clear)
- Red, scaly patch on breast skin or areola
- Breast or nipple pain not related to menstrual cycle

**Later-Stage Symptoms:**
- Breast pain that doesn't go away
- Swelling in lymph nodes under arm or around collarbone
- Bone pain (if spread to skeleton)
- Headaches or neurological symptoms (if spread to brain)
- Jaundice or abdominal pain (if spread to liver)
- Shortness of breath or persistent cough (if spread to lungs)
- Extreme fatigue and unexplained weight loss

## 3. Colorectal Cancer

**Early Symptoms:**
- Changes in bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or narrowing of stool)
- Blood in stool - bright red or very dark
- Feeling that bowel doesn't empty completely
- Rectal bleeding
- Persistent abdominal discomfort (cramps, gas, pain)
- Unexplained weight loss (less common in early stages)

**Later-Stage Symptoms:**
- Severe abdominal pain and cramping
- Iron deficiency anemia (fatigue, weakness, pale skin)
- Significant, unintentional weight loss
- Nausea and vomiting
- Bowel obstruction (inability to pass stool or gas)
- Swelling in abdomen due to fluid buildup
- Jaundice (if cancer spreads to liver)
- Shortness of breath (if cancer spreads to lungs)

## 4. Stomach Cancer

**Early Symptoms:**
- Often minimal or no symptoms in very early stages
- Indigestion or heartburn that doesn't respond to treatment
- Loss of appetite, especially for meat
- Bloating after meals
- Mild nausea or stomach discomfort
- Feeling full quickly when eating

**Later-Stage Symptoms:**
- Significant, unintentional weight loss
- Severe stomach pain
- Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
- Blood in stool (black, tarry stool)
- Difficulty swallowing
- Yellowing of skin and eyes (jaundice)
- Swelling or fluid buildup in abdomen
- Extreme fatigue and weakness
- Palpable lump or mass in abdomen

## 5. Liver Cancer

**Early Symptoms:**
- Often asymptomatic in early stages
- Vague right upper abdominal discomfort
- Loss of appetite
- Unexplained weight loss
- General feeling of unwellness (malaise)
- Mild fatigue

**Later-Stage Symptoms:**
- Noticeable lump or pain in right side below rib cage
- Swelling of abdomen (ascites)
- Yellowish skin and eyes (jaundice)
- Easy bruising or bleeding
- Dark urine and pale stools
- Significant weight loss and muscle wasting
- Confusion or changes in mental status (due to liver failure)
- Severe fatigue and weakness
- Fever (occasionally)
- Itching (pruritus)

## Important Notes for Women:

1. **Know Your Body**: Pay attention to changes that persist for more than 2-3 weeks
2. **Don't Ignore Symptoms**: Many early cancer symptoms can be mistaken for less serious conditions
3. **Screening is Key**: Some cancers like breast and colorectal cancer have effective screening tests
4. **Family History Matters**: Women with family history of these cancers should be especially vigilant
5. **Risk Factors**: Smoking, obesity, excessive alcohol consumption, and certain infections increase risk

**When to See a Doctor**: Women should seek medical attention if they experience any persistent or worsening symptoms, especially if they have risk factors for these cancers. Early detection significantly improves treatment outcomes for all these cancer types.

- Skin dimpling or puckering (like orange peel)
- Nipple changes: turning inward, scaling, or crusting
- Nipple discharge (especially bloody or clear)
- Red, scaly patch on breast skin
- Breast or nipple pain not related to menstrual cycle

**Later-Stage Symptoms:**
- Swelling in lymph nodes under arm or collarbone
- Bone pain, headaches, or neurological symptoms
- Jaundice or abdominal pain (if spread)
- Extreme fatigue and unexplained weight loss

- Persistent abdominal discomfort
- Unexplained weight loss (less common early)

**Later-Stage Symptoms:**
- Iron deficiency anemia (fatigue, weakness, pale skin)
- Significant unintentional weight loss
- Nausea and vomiting
- Bowel obstruction
- Jaundice (if liver spread)

## **4. Stomach Cancer**

**Early Symptoms:**
- Often minimal symptoms initially
- Indigestion or heartburn not responding to treatment

- Feeling full quickly when eating

- Difficulty swallowing
- Yellowing skin and eyes (jaundice)

- Often asymptomatic initially

- Loss of appetite and unexplained weight loss
- General feeling of unwellness (malaise)

- Noticeable lump or pain in right side below ribs

- Confusion or mental status changes
